chunks: Abu Nasr Hibatullah ibn Muhammad ibn Ahmad al-Katib, son of the daughter of Umm Kulthum bint Abi Ja'far Muhammad ibn Uthman al-Amiri, may Allah be pleased with him, said that Abu Dalf Muhammad ibn Muzaffar al-Katib was, at the beginning of his affair, a Mukhammas and known for that, because he was the upbringing, student, and creation of the Kharkhis, and the Kharkhis were Mukhammas, no one from the Shias doubted that. And indeed Abu Dalf used to say that and acknowledge it, and he would say: 'Our master, the virtuous Shaykh, may Allah sanctify his soul and the light of his shrine, transferred me from the creed of Abu Ja'far al-Karikhi to the correct creed,' meaning the belief of Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi.

key_terms.أَبُو بَكْرٍ الْبَغْدَادِيُّ: Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi, a prominent early Shia scholar and deputy
key_terms.الْكَرْخِيِّينَ: The Kharkhis, a prominent family of Shia scribes and scholars
key_terms.مُخَمَّسًا: Mukhammas, a follower of the Four Deputies of the Imam

ai.seo_question: Who was Abu Dalf and what was his religious affiliation before converting to the mainstream Shia view?
ai.summary: This narration from Al-Tusi’s *Kitab al-Ghayba* highlights the sectarian fluidity of early Shia scribes, specifically Abu Dalf, who transitioned from the 'Mukhammas' (followers of the Four Deputies) tradition of the Kharki family to the mainstream Twelver belief under the guidance of a virtuous Shaykh. It underscores the historical context of the Kufan scholarly milieu, where identity was often tied to specific scholarly lineages rather than rigid dogmatic boundaries, illustrating the organic development of Twelhi orthodoxy.
